content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes AttendOut, which adopts the idea of meta-learning, to dynamically (in contrast to static vanilla dropout) drop the units in the attention matrix. The experimental results on various NLP datasets show that AttendOut yields improvement over various baselines.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

1. The proposed approach achieves better performance on various NLP datasets. (But I also have concerns about the clarity.)



Weaknesses:

1. The motivation of the utilization of LSTM for modeling is not clear. Why should it be modeled in a temporal manner? 
2. The paper suffers from clarity issues, such as the experimental setups, descriptions of the results, etc. Also, some of the claims are not convincing. Please see my comments in the next section.
3. The authors claim that AttendOut features `faster tuning circle` in the abstract, but I did not see a specific analysis on this point.



Comments:

1. Eq 2: Why is it scaled by 1/p? The original implementation in BERT does not apply 1/p scaling here.
2. Section 4.1: `we assume ... between two models.` What are the `two models`?
3. The paper does not say which version of BERT and RoBERTa were adopted. Base or large? Cased or uncased? Please be specific in illustrating your experimental setups.
4. In Section 6.1, it is not clear how these numbers are calculated and why you use `relative growth rate` here? I tried to calculate one of them but failed to give the exact numbers. In this context, I can only rely on the results in Table 1 and 2, away from the distracting descriptions in Section 6.1.
5. Figure 1: How about the curves in the top-most layer (closest to the output)? Also, why is there only one curve in STS-B? I don't think all four curves are identical.
6. Figure 2: You mentioned that `we can see more steady declines in AttendOut case`. However, the observation is only clear in Figure 2b, but not in others. Maybe you should provide some statistics (such as variance) to support this claim.
7. Figure 3: Please be more specific to describe the `experiment ID` and its real setting, but not only leave a sentence like `the experiment IDs are in order as they are mentioned`.
content.summary_of_the_review: In the current stage, I cannot vote for accepting this paper due to the unclear motivation and clarity issues, which hinder me from understanding this paper properly. The authors are encouraged to improve their writing and be more specific in illustrating technical content.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer #4
content.comment:
We highly appreciate for your helpful feedback on our paper. We will answer your question one by one bellow and meanwhile update the revision.

**Why LSTM**

Thank you for your question. We are sorry for omitting this part in our paper and very willing to add the analysis in Appendix.

We previously try MLP-based modeling in our last version, which we submitted to NeurIPS 2022. It also works and achieves competitive results. We show part of the results here. You can also refer to [https://openreview.net/forum?id=rdT5GV-LnZU] for the complete experimental results.

| Model | CoLA | SST-2 | QNLI | MNLI-m/mm | RTE | STS-B |
| :--- | :----: | :----: | :----: | :----: | :----: | :----: |
| BERT | 51.9 | 92.9 | 89.7 | 84.3/83.6 | 67.4 | 84.6 |
| MLP | 57.4 | 93.6 | 90.2 | 84.6/84.2 | 69.8 | 85.2 |
| LSTM | 57.4 | 93.9 | 90.6 | 84.6/83.8 | 70.4 | 85.6 |

It turns out that our proposed optimization objective is general under different modeling manner, while we can see LSTM-base modeling performs better.

There is another contributed factor why we choose LSTM. We assume that the dropout proportion is related to the training and evaluation losses, to prevent the situation when model fits well on training points but behaves worse on unseen ones (Section 4.1). For example, the training loss is continually down, while the evaluation loss is up. LSTM is able to model such trend in a few steps but MLP cannot which merely cares about the moment.

It is highly necessary to supplement this part. We will add this part in Appendix. Thank you so much!

**Faster tuning circle**

We discuss this part in our further study (Section 8 “Tuning AttendOut”). We try 8 different settings for Vanilla Dropout as well as 4 values of K for AttendOut to make fair comparison. In Figure 3, we can see AttendOut (red bars) takes a higher tolerance rate since the average performances (grey lines) are always higher on all three tasks.

Additionally, tuning dropout probabilities for all attention layers requires far more trials than 8, while only 4 are what we need using AttendOut, which leads to a faster tuning circle.

**Scaled by 1/p**

There is 1/p in the original implementation of BERT but it is packaged in PyTorch “nn.Dropout”. Such implementation is consistent with that in Vanilla Dropout [1].

We will specify this part to avoid ambiguity. Thank you!

**“Two models” in “we assume that dropout acts as another connection between two models”**

The “two models” here refers to the models at two steps $ t $ and $ t+1 $. They are supposed to have different dropout proportion $ D_t $ and $ D_{t+1} $. We have modified this part to make it easier to understand. Thank you!

**BERT and RoBERTa version**

Thank you for your reminder. We utilize “bert-base-uncased” and “roberta-base” checkpoints of Huggingface repo. We will mention this part in the footnote in Section 5.

**Relative growth rate in Section 6.1**

We use relative percentage in our significance analysis in Tab 1 and Tab 2. For example, on RTE: 67.4 and 70.4 -> (70.4 - 67.4) / 67.4 = 4.5%, on SST-2: 92.9 and 93.9 -> 1 / 92.9 = 1.1%. We have specified this part in the new revision.

**Curves of top-most layer**

We use base-size model in our experiments, which contains 12 attention layers. We uniformly take four attention layers for conciseness. We will depict the other layers latter in Appendix. Thank you!

**Curves of STS-B**

The four curves are almost identical (overlap in the figure) learning through AttendOut. As training proceeds, they do become identical since all equal to 1.0. We run the experiment for times and obtain similar results. Even if intermittently using AttendOut and Vanilla Dropout, the results are almost the same as in Figure 6 (c). We speculate that dropout patterns differ from task to task (Section 6.2). For semantic similarity task, the optimized dropout proportion is much lower.

**Steady decline in Figure 2**

Sorry for the improper expression in our paper. We are meant to say that the evaluation loss as training proceeds is lower in AttendOut case, which indicates the effectiveness of our meta-learning framework. We will modify the expression in the new revision. Thank you!

**Experiment ID in Figure 3**

The experiment IDs from 1-5 refer to the dropout probabilities in {0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4} for Vanilla dropout. The IDs 6, 7, 8 refer to “0.1 for the first layer and 0 for the rest”, “0.2 for the first and 0 for the rest”, “0.1 for the first 0.2 for the second and 0 for the rest”. We have specified this part in the caption.

Greatly appreciate for you careful corrections! For all the issues above, we will clarify them in our new revision.

[1] Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting

display_title: Official Review of Paper2952 by Reviewer Vene

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this work, the authors propose to apply meta-learning so that the dropouts in self-attention networks can be done in a unit-specific way. The proposed mechanism leverages Policy Gradients for learning, and several experiments have shown that this method should be applied to many network architectures for language models.
content.main_review:
# Summarization

In this work, the authors propose that in self-attention networks, the performance can benefit from dropouts being  “smarter”, e.g. unit-specific. The author proposes to leverage the meta-learning framework and model the dropout as the update of LSTM cells.

# Strong Points
This is an interesting problem to study. The authors challenge the view of having a uniformed dropout, which is a widely used practice. The author also shows interesting experiments including showing the significance and convergences, as well as ablation studies (a good job!) 

# Weak Points
 I found many issues (listed below) in the manuscript in its current form. Such issues should be addressed before readers can better understand the proposed method’s contributions.

1. The narrative is relatively poor and needs improvement.
    - The writing itself is not fully self-containing in a way that there are several mental gaps that need to be filled by looking at the referred paper. For example, the proposed use of  meta-learning in Section 4.1 and 4.2 is poorly explained and readers need to refer to [1] where it was originally proposed for details (even for the meaning of symbols).
    - There are many missing details. For example,it remains unclear what are the dimensionalities of variables in Section 4.1., and how the formulate in Section 4.1 is instantiated for multiple layers.

2. The technical novelty is limited. The meta-learning is mostly a verbatim account from [1] and other referred works (to a lesser extent). Thus in my understanding, the contribution is limited to applying the gradient policy (a well-known technique) for training.

3. there are also several issues with the experiments:
    - For fine-tuning, only three runs with random seeds are used for calculating the confidence level. Given the large reported std in Table 2, it may not be sufficient, and I would suggest that the authors have more runs.
    - Comparison with vanilla dropout is missing. Since this manuscript argues for the superiority of “smart” dropout over vanilla dropout, a comparison with basic vanilla dropout would be helpful. I understand that the analysis into the *combination* with vanilla dropout is provided, however that may not shed the full light.

# Assessment
Given the issues in narrative, limited technical novelty, and issues in the experiments, I would suggest rejecting as the manuscript in its current form is not good enough.

# Additional Comments

I would suggest the authors further proofread the writing. 

# Reference
[1] Sachin Ravi and Hugo Larochelle, 2017: Optimization as a model for few-shot learning.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given the issues in narrative, limited technical novelty, and issues in the experiments, I would suggest rejecting as the manuscript in its current form is not good enough.

content.title: Clarification of paper impact
content.comment:
Sorry for the long time to update all results in our new revision. Only two submissions are allowed per day on GLUE website. We run another three random seeds as you mentioned above. Thank you for your patience.

**Clarification of paper impact**

Meta-learning is a kind of general-purpose machine learning technique, for which we utilize to solve our concerned problem. For the sake of practice on large pre-trained language models, we propose a novel dropout objective and enable its learning through policy gradient. However, this paper is contributed for the broad impact of its concerned task object rather than developing brand new meta-learning method. Stronger attention dropout facilitates Transformer-based models, which are widely used or even dominate the cut-edge NLP, CV as well as graph computation. More specifically, it unfolds a much more effective training manner of any pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa), the star role in the state-of-the-art natural language processing, which achieve remarkable success in a mass of downstream tasks. 

We promise to release our code to facilitate other researches and engineers.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2952 by Reviewer Ccb6

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to selectively adjust dropout rates which are governed by LSTM-based meta-networks for transformer-based language models. The meta-networks is "nearly parameter-free" compared to transformer models since it only concerns relatively small attention matrices. To reduce the computational cost due to a second-order optimization problem while meta-training the meta-networks, they exploit REINFORCE algorithm (Williams, 1992) and Gumbel-Sigmoid estimator (Maddison et al., 2014).
content.main_review:
### Strength

**Better performances for BERT and RoBERTa.** The proposed method consistently outperforms the GLUE benchmark. Some results show significant improvement over their baselines. This work gives insight into the attention dropout in transformer networks in an aspect of meta-learning.

### Weakness

**W1. Unclear additional computational cost.** The most huddle to use this method in practice is the additional computational cost from meta-learning. Even if the meta-networks have *nearly parameter-free*, it involves K inner-step updates of task parameters which linearly increase memory footprints as shown in Figure 7 and presumably linearly increase the number of steps to converge the training curves. In a situation where abundant training data, this method compensates the number of training steps for large dataset significantly. For a strictly fair comparison, could you include the performance comparison where the training time or effective training steps is controlled?

**W2. Weights Dropout and Scores Dropout is not equal.** Since the weights dropout applies the mask over the probability distribution which is summed to one, it makes that is no longer normalized where the sum is one. The 1/p does not recover this probability distribution. While the scores dropout applies to before the softmax function, it strictly maintains the probability distribution is normalized where the sum is one. Since the vanilla transformers use the weights dropout while the proposed method uses the scores dropout, there is some discrepancy applying attention dropout. The authors should clarify this difference is not significant, otherwise, the experiments are not fairly compared actually.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is reasonably well-written and gives a good explanation of their idea. Only the hindered to recommend this paper strongly is W1) unclear additional computational cost from meta-learning steps, and wrong explanation on the difference between W2) weights dropout and scores dropout. W1 would be a significant huddle to adopt this method in practice, and W2 leaves a question on the fair comparison with competitive methods, although this would be a minor issue.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer #2
content.comment:
Highly appreciate for your advice!

**Additional computational cost**

The proposed meta-learning framework linearly increases the memory footprints as in Figure 7. However, we do not reuse the samples in the one batch for the inner training to control the training time, so the number of the training steps remains the same. Besides, in the situation of abundant training data, we conduct uniform sampling on the dev set or use a smaller validation set to guarantee the efficiency. We compare the training efficiency and performance bellow.

| BERT | MRPC | RTE | STS-B |
| :--- | :----: | :----: | :----: |
| BERT | 87.2 | 67.4 | 84.6 |
| +AttendOut | 87.8 (x1.38) | 70.4 (x1.24) | 85.2 (x1.52) |

Our empirical experiments show that the main difference of time consumption comes from the size of validation set to meta-test on.

We also add this part in Appendix C. Considering it takes at least twice as long to tune dropout probability of each layer, the computation cost of self-adjusting dropout is acceptable.

**Two formats of attention dropout**

The implementation of weights dropout is consistent with that in Vanilla dropout [1]. The 1/p ensures that for any hidden unit the expected output is the same as the actual output, even thought the sum is no longer 1, which is a little weird.

Besides, we empirically find same dropout probabilities under weights and scores dropout lead to similar performances on downstream tasks. That is why we merely apply scores dropout in our study. We have clarified this issue in the new version. Thank you so much!

[1] Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes the AttndOut method, which is a meta-learning algorithm that learns how to dropout the attention weight matrix. The method is inspired by LSTM and consist of a forget gate and an input gate. The authors conducted experiments on various datasets to verify the effectiveness of this method.
content.main_review:
Strength:
-	The idea that adaptively change the dropout is a good point.
-	The authors conducted experiments on various datasets.
-	Not too much extra parameters for model.

Weakness:
-	The title is confusing. What the paper is trying to do is just drop some attention weight, not get rid of attention mechanism.
-	The motivation is the common dropout is predefined for all hidden layers. However, it’s not clear why the proposed meta-learning method is only applied to attention dropout. Although attention dropout is important for Transformer, other dropout layers in Transformer are also not neglectable and can be handled by same way.
-	In Equation (7), the subscript s is not in the summed formula. More explanation of it is required. 
-	In the Table 3, the result of Scheduled Bernoulli on RTE is even better than AttendOut. What is the reason that AttendOut has lower variance? What is the statistical significance value when comparing Scheduled Bernoulli and AttendOut?
content.summary_of_the_review:
I recommend rejecting because:
-	The reason why the proposed meta-learning method is only applicable to attention dropout not other dropout layers, is not clear.
-	Improvement over the Scheduled Bernoulli baseline is limited, which makes the importance of LSTM questionable.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer #1
content.comment:
We highly appreciate for your helpful feedback on our paper. We will answer your question one by one bellow and update the revision.

**Title**

Thank you so much. We have not come up with a better title at this moment, while we will carefully consider your advice. If you have any suggestion on the title, please tell us. Thank you!

**Not use on other dropout layers**

Yes, it is correct that the proposed dropout can be applied on other layers in Transformer (under modest modification). However, BERT-base undertakes 104M units. Since our method is unit-specific dropout, current devices do not have enough graph memory to apply gradient descent on each of the units. Thus, we pick out the attention layer, the basic architecture of Transformer to conduct dropout. Besides, vast literature demonstrates the effectiveness of attention dropout, even though they all rely on prior knowledge or have a huge search space. We aim to design a smart self-adjusting one instead.

We will clarify this part in our motivation. Thank you!

**Equation (7)**

Thank you for your reminder. The subscript $ s $ refers to the in-batch samples of model training. For conciseness, we omit it in $ d^{ij}_t $, which actually refers to the dropout for each sample ($ s=1 \sim m $) in the batch. We have specified this part in the new revision.

**The results of scheduled Bernoulli dropout**

It makes sense that scheduled Bernoulli dropout is quite closer (even better on RTE) to AttendOut, since the scheduler pattern is inverse-engineered from AttendOut, that is we calculate the instantaneous dropout rate of AttendOut and modify the p of Vanilla dropout (implemented with Bernoulli distribution). If we do not apply AttendOut to learn the latent dropout pattern, there is no idea to get to the optimized dropout scheduler. We design this experiment to demonstrate the correctness of the learned dropout pattern by AttendOut as well as the regularization effect of it.

We give the GLUE test results for supplement. We see that AttendOut is consistently better than scheduled Bernoulli on test set.

| Model | MRPC | RTE | STS-B |
| :--- | :----: | :----: | :----: |
| BERT | 87.2 | 67.4 | 84.6 |
| +scheduler | 87.5 | 69.3 | 85.0 |
| +AttendOut | 87.8 | 70.4 | 85.6 |

We will further clarify this part to let it easier to understand. Thank you so much!

**Lower variance of AttendOut**

In most cases, the dropout proportion brought by AttendOut is higher. We speculate that a more intensive regularizer might help reduce the variance. We mention this part in the Appendix A.1.

We conduct further experiments on RTE test to empirically verify this speculation, where we apply 0.5 attention dropout rate on BERT-base and run five random seeds.

| Model | Seed 1 | Seed 2 | Seed 3 | Seed 4 | Seed 5 |
| :--- | :----: | :----: | :----: | :----: | :----: |
| BERT | 66.2 | 65.4 | 65.6 | 66.5 | 65.1 | 65.0 |
